questions.question: What does enabling 'Apply Transformations' do when exporting a GLB from Blender?
options: Bakes any pending scale, rotation, and location transforms into the mesh data
Converts the model from Z-up to Y-up axis orientation
Embeds all linked textures into the binary file
Applies Draco compression to the mesh geometry
questions.explanation: Apply Transformations bakes any pending transform values into the mesh so the model arrives in Three.js with clean, applied transforms rather than unexpected scale factors.

questions.question: You run `npx gltf-transform inspect input.glb` and see a 12 MB file with a 4096x4096 texture. What is the best next step?
options: Reload the model in Three.js - the file size is fine for web
Resize the texture to 1024x1024 with gltf-transform before optimizing
Switch from GLB to GLTF format to reduce size
Increase the Draco compression ratio in Blender's export settings
questions.explanation: A 4096x4096 texture is oversized for most web assets. Running `npx gltf-transform resize --width 1024 --height 1024` before optimizing will dramatically reduce file size.

questions.question: Which Blender modifier is most useful for reducing polygon count before web export?
options: Subdivision Surface - adds more geometry for smoother shapes
Mirror - duplicates geometry across an axis
Solidify - adds thickness to flat surfaces
Decimate - reduces face count while preserving overall shape
questions.explanation: The Decimate modifier reduces polygon count while trying to preserve the overall shape. Setting the Ratio to 0.3-0.5 can bring a high-poly AI mesh down to web-friendly levels.

questions.question: What is the key reason to choose GLB format over GLTF+Bin when exporting for the web?
options: GLB supports more material types than GLTF
GLB files are automatically Draco-compressed on export
GLB packs all geometry, textures, and materials into a single binary file
GLB is faster to export from Blender than other formats
questions.explanation: GLB is the binary form of GLTF that packs everything (geometry, materials, textures) into a single file. GLTF+Bin splits data across multiple files, making web deployment more complex.

questions.question: A model loads in Three.js but appears lying on its back instead of standing upright. What is the most likely fix?
options: Add DRACOLoader - the model failed to decompress correctly
Enable Draco in the Blender export settings and re-export
Apply the model scale to 0.01 in Three.js code
Rotate the model -90 degrees on the X axis in Three.js or fix the axis in Blender before export
questions.explanation: Blender uses Z as the up axis; GLTF and Three.js use Y. Even though the exporter usually handles this, models can arrive rotated. The fix is model.rotation.x = -Math.PI / 2 in Three.js, or applying the correction in Blender.
